questions.question: What real-world patterns do you use when consuming APIs in production (sessions, retries, rate limits)?
questions.title: Real-World API Consumption Patterns
questions.direct_answer: Production API consumption uses four patterns beyond a single get: (1) Sessions — a requests.Session() reuses the TCP connection and cookies across calls (faster, and keeps auth/headers set once); (2) Retries with backoff — retry transient failures (timeouts, 429, 5xx) with exponential backoff, via urllib3 Retry or a loop; (3) Rate-limit handling — respect Retry-After on 429 and cap your request rate; (4) Pagination — loop over paginated endpoints, collecting results until an empty page. These turn a one-off call into robust, efficient, polite API consumption.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you name the four production patterns (sessions, retries, rate limits, pagination) and why each matters — not just 'use requests.get'.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Calling requests.get in a loop without a session (slow, no connection reuse) or retrying a 404 (won't fix).
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Four patterns: Session (reuse conn/cookies), retries with backoff (transient only), rate-limit/Retry-After (be polite), pagination (loop pages).

sections.title: What the interviewer wants
sections.content: Define Real-World API Consumption Patterns simply, show a small example, and mention the main trade-off or edge case.

sections.title: Beyond the One-Off Call
sections.content: Production API consumption uses patterns beyond a single requests.get. (1) Sessions: a requests.Session() reuses the underlying TCP connection and cookies across calls, which is faster (connection reuse) and lets you set auth/headers once. (2) Retries with backoff: retry transient failures (timeouts, 429, 5xx) with exponential backoff — don't retry 4xx client errors, which won't fix by retrying. Use urllib3's Retry or a loop with time.sleep. (3) Rate-limit handling: respect the Retry-After header on 429 and cap your request rate to be a polite client. (4) Pagination: loop over paginated endpoints, collecting results until an empty page or a cursor runs out. These turn a one-off call into robust, efficient, polite API consumption.

sections.title: The Four Production Patterns
sections.content:
Sessions reuse connections; retries handle transient failures; rate limits keep you polite; pagination loops results.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  S[Session: reuse conn + cookies] --> Fast[faster calls]
  R[Retry w/ backoff on 429/5xx/timeout] --> Robust[robust to transients]
  L[Respect Retry-After / cap rate] --> Polite[polite client]
  P[Pagination loop] --> All[all results]
```

sections.title: Session, retry, rate-limit, and pagination
sections.content:
```python
import requests, time
from urllib3.util.retry import Retry
from requests.adapters import HTTPAdapter

# (1) SESSION: reuse the connection; set auth/headers once.
s = requests.Session()
s.headers['Authorization'] = f'Bearer {token}'

# (2) RETRIES with backoff: mount a Retry adapter on the session.
retry = Retry(total=3, backoff_factor=0.5,
              status_forcelist=[429, 500, 502, 503, 504])
s.mount('https://', HTTPAdapter(max_retries=retry))

# (3) RATE LIMIT: on 429, wait Retry-After before retrying (Retry handles this).
#   Also cap your own rate (e.g., a token bucket) to be a polite client.

# (4) PAGINATION: loop pages until empty.
page = 1; all_items = []
while True:
    r = s.get(url, params={'page': page})
    items = r.json()
    if not items: break
    all_items.extend(items); page += 1
```

sections.title: Common Mistakes
items: Using requests.get in a loop without a session — slow (no connection reuse), no shared cookies.
Retrying a 4xx (client error) — it won't fix by retrying; only retry transient failures (429/5xx/timeout).
Ignoring 429/Retry-After and hammering the server — you'll get banned; back off and wait.

sections.title: Key Takeaways
items: Use a Session to reuse connections/cookies and set auth/headers once — faster than repeated get() calls.
Retry transient failures (timeout, 429, 5xx) with exponential backoff; don't retry 4xx.
Respect the Retry-After header on 429 and cap your request rate to be a polite client.
Paginate: loop pages (or follow a cursor) until an empty page or the cursor runs out.
Always set a timeout on every call so a hung server doesn't block you.

sections.title: Spoken Answer
sections.content: Production API consumption uses patterns beyond a single requests dot get. Sessions: a requests dot Session reuses the underlying TCP connection and cookies across calls, which is faster through connection reuse and lets you set auth and headers once. Retries with backoff: retry transient failures — timeouts, 429, and 5xx — with exponential backoff, and don't retry 4xx client errors, which won't fix by retrying; use urllib3's Retry or a loop with time dot sleep. Rate-limit handling: respect the Retry-After header on 429 and cap your request rate to be a polite client, because hammering a server gets you banned. Pagination: loop over paginated endpoints, collecting results until an empty page or a cursor runs out. These turn a one-off call into robust, efficient, polite API consumption. The common mistakes are using requests.get in a loop without a session, which is slow and has no shared cookies, retrying a 4xx which won't fix by retrying, and ignoring 429 and Retry-After.
